newsitem.title: GERMANY: WAIGEL SAYS NO SENSE IN DISCUSSING EMU DELAY.
newsitem.headline: WAIGEL SAYS NO SENSE IN DISCUSSING EMU DELAY.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Saturday it was counterproductive to discuss a delay in the start of European monetary union (EMU), set for January 1, 1999.
"It does not make sense to discuss a delay in currency union," Waigel told reporters.

Waigel said a discussion about delaying the start of currency union would only create unrest in financial markets. He also said such a decision must be made by the European Union council of ministers.

Waigel's comments come after Germany's Der Spiegel magazine said on Saturday that Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer has asked whether Germany and France can consider delaying the start of EMU if they fail to meet entry criteria in 1997.
"Wouldn't it be a possibility, together with France, to agree to a delay in the start of the euro?" the magazine quoted Tietmeyer as saying in an article to be published this week.

Spiegel, citing unnamed sources, said in the article released ahead of publication that Tietmeyer did not believe it would be wrong if currency union were delayed if Bonn and Paris did not meet entry criteria this year for the 1999 start.

Prospects for a delay have risen after Bonn and the Bundesbank last week openly clashed over Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plans to revalue the bank's reserves and demand a payout of the hidden profits to help Bonn meet the criteria.
The Bundesbank, a fierce proponent of fiscal austerity in meeting the criteria for monetary union, on Wednesday openly critcised Waigel's plan and said it could undermine the euro from the start.
Waigel has said his plan does not attack the Bundesbank's independence and that the bank agreed with him on the need to value the reserves of gold and currencies towards market prices.
